Core research question: What documentary traces connect Job 171, "Designer-computer interaction in the early stages of design”, to the people, activities and outputs associated with it?
Primary stress test: Multi-document reconstruction; whether retrieval can assemble people, activity and outputs around a known archival anchor.
What retrieval surfaced: Live archive-first retrieval selected five Docling passages from the April 1977 Job 171 records 171/06 and 171/07. They directly describe interface-design activities including hardware design, selection and training, job-aid design, procedure specification and job specification; human-factors considerations for computer users; man-computer dialogue criteria; and CEDAR Mark 2, a prototype computer-aided building-design system developed by the Department of the Environment in conjunction with the Royal College of Art. The Job 171 authority identifies the project title, Science Research Council funding and Pierre Goumain as project lead.
What the model inferred: the model's final synthesis retained the direct Job 171 record excerpts and identified the interface-design and CEDAR Mark 2 material. It treated Pierre Goumain as authority context rather than direct documentary evidence, made no cross-source inference, and stated that no direct claim about a specific individual's activity beyond the selected descriptions was established.
What was useful: The project-record extension to the deterministic compiler now preserves exact documentary passages where a question supplies an explicit Job number, even though no named individual appears in the passage. All five final documentary claims passed chunk and quotation provenance validation. This makes the archive-record identity, documentary content and authority context inspectable as separate layers.
What was overstated/flattened: The final wording still uses the broad phrase that the documents connect Job 171 to people, activities and outputs. The connection to the project is archival record identity; the passages do not establish Pierre Goumain's involvement in a particular activity or output, nor that CEDAR Mark 2 was itself a Job 171 output.
Missingness: The selected documents directly establish the stated interface-design concerns, dialogue criteria and the CEDAR Mark 2 description within records identified as Job 171. They do not establish authorship, responsibility or participation by Pierre Goumain or another specific person; a complete people/activity/output reconstruction; or that CEDAR Mark 2 was commissioned, produced or delivered by Job 171. The 1977 material predates the June 1985 DDR closure boundary.
Research significance: Q01 demonstrates project-level evidence control: an authority record can identify a project and lead, archive metadata can associate selected records with that project, and exact Docling passages can establish their own technical content without collapsing those layers into a claim of individual responsibility or project output.
Notes: Live production verification on 2026-09-07 after commits b29c25b and 3e0cffe. Selected records: Job 171/06 and 171/07; final direct-claim provenance passed for five citations. Project authority is supplied to the model as administrative context only; the June 1985 closure guard is active.

Core research question: How is Bruce Archer’s role in teaching and learning practice with students represented across multiple DDR documents, and what aspects of that role are directly evidenced rather than inferred?
Primary stress test: Retrieval versus inference; whether the model distinguishes documented activity from its own synthesis.
What retrieval surfaced: The live archive-first retrieval surfaced the Frank Height memo to Bruce Archer (asset PID 852120727979, page 2), Professor Archer course material, and an Archer lecture. The memo directly records an alternative arrangement involving Department of Design Research courses, 'your own lectures and tutorials,' and a computer course. Current DDR GraphQL enrichment supplies the V&A East Storehouse repository, AU.AAD.20747 accession, location note, copyright, image rights and data rights for the source card.
What the model inferred: the model identified the 16 April 1975 Height memo as direct evidence that Archer provided lectures and tutorials. It treated a broader teaching-and-learning role with students across the source set as an interpretation rather than claiming that the complete role was directly established.
What was useful: The staged pipeline now preserves the exact page-2 documentary excerpt before synthesis, so direct evidence cannot disappear when the model omits a Stage A claim. The response also distinguishes the specific direct teaching trace from the broader cross-document interpretation and exposes the authoritative source metadata required for inspection.
What was overstated/flattened: The response still compresses the course and lecture records into a broad statement that no further direct evidence is provided. Those records require document-by-document reading before they can support a fuller account of Archer's teaching role or student-facing practice.
Missingness: The retained evidence directly establishes lectures and tutorials in the proposed 1975 arrangement. It does not yet establish Archer's complete pedagogy, teaching method, supervision practices, students' experience, teaching effectiveness, educational outcomes, or a complete reconstruction of his role. These are bounded documentary limits, not archival absence.
Research significance: Q02 demonstrates the repaired architecture: archive-first retrieval selects the relevant source family; deterministic extraction preserves exact documentary relations; the model provides a constrained interpretation; and live DDR GraphQL enrichment makes the citation, rights and location data inspectable in the UI.
Notes: Live production verification on 2026-09-07 after commits c93b93e, 2c7f067, 2ff47ea and 1edff39. Direct evidence: chunk_66a2824c026302cf, page 2; final direct-claim provenance passed. Catalogue enrichment is display/provenance only and is not supplied to the model.

Core research question: What evidence connects Ken Baynes and Phil Roberts within the work of the Design Education Unit?
Primary stress test: Relationship synthesis across dispersed records; whether a connection can be reconstructed without exaggerating its significance.
What retrieval surfaced: Live GraphQL record 014262507600 identifies a June 1978 Design Education Unit attached-media record (PID 287080879712) whose controlled keywords include both Ken Baynes and Phil Roberts. The corrected archive-first retrieval selected distinct DEU assets headed by Phil Roberts and Ken Baynes, plus one Design Dimension proposed-publications page that jointly credits them for 'Design as a medium for learning.'
What the model inferred: The final answer is deterministic for this typed evidence shape. It identifies the shared controlled-keyword association, names the selected Roberts and Baynes DEU assets, and distinguishes the separate documentary joint credit. The model contributes no relationship inference.
What was useful: The answer now uses the catalogue assertion that actually connects the pair, rather than treating three accidental co-mentions as the whole answer. It keeps the parent record/attachment association explicitly archival metadata and preserves the joint-credit page as one provenance-validated documentary claim.
What was overstated/flattened: A shared controlled keyword association is an archival description, not proof that the two people collaborated, co-authored material or shared responsibility. The selected asset titles identify archival records and do not make their contents direct evidence until their pages are read.
Missingness: The evidence establishes a shared DEU archival association and one joint attribution. It does not establish collaboration, co-authorship, shared responsibility, either person's full DEU role, or DDR activity after the June 1985 closure boundary.
Research significance: This case demonstrates why structured archival metadata must be a first-class, separately typed evidence layer. Excluding it makes a relationship question appear under-evidenced; treating it as documentary text would overstate it.
Notes: Validated in production after refreshing 24 DEU snapshot assets with inherited parent controlled keywords. Five sources include distinct Roberts and Baynes assets; one direct documentary claim has valid chunk/quotation provenance; no inferences. Deployments: 552eb0b, 5eb0cd2, 43e185e, ed6fbc3.

Core research question: How is John Wood’s role in console design and ergonomics documented across different DDR source types?
Primary stress test: Cross-source retrieval; whether different document types contribute complementary rather than duplicated evidence.
What retrieval surfaced: The corrected person-and-topic supplement selected two near-duplicate 1975 DDR course listings and a separate circa-1982 DDR brochure. The course listings name John Wood in the Ergonomics Course, assign '(JW)' to the introductory lecture on ergonomics, and assign '(JW)' to 'Ergonomics and the design of computer consoles for emergency services.' The brochure lists Wood with Douglas Tomkin for the 1973 Police command and control consoles project, DDR/146.
What the model inferred: The final synthesis used the three deterministic documentary claims. It states that the course records assign Wood the ergonomics introduction and the emergency-services computer-console case study, while the brochure attributes him and Douglas Tomkin to the 1973 police-console project. It made no cross-source inference.
What was useful: The generic single-person/topic supplement fixed a retrieval failure that previously selected calendars and an invitation but no console record. The evidence compiler now retains later material clauses in a passage and matches singular question terms to plural documentary forms, so the exact computer-console assignment and police-console attribution survive synthesis.
What was overstated/flattened: The two 1975 course records are substantively near-duplicates, not independent confirmation. The evidence supports course and project attributions, not an unqualified claim that Wood alone designed the consoles or a complete ergonomic role. The separate 1973 and 1975 records should not be collapsed into one continuous responsibility claim.
Missingness: The selected records do not establish Wood's precise responsibilities, the division of work with Douglas Tomkin or other course contributors, the design outcome of the police consoles, or a complete chronology of his role. They cannot establish DDR activity after the June 1985 closure boundary.
Research significance: This case validates source-type diversity and demonstrates that documentary extraction must preserve material text beyond an initial matching term. It also keeps related records distinct: a curriculum assigns teaching/case-study activity, while a brochure supplies a project attribution.
Notes: Validated in production: three deterministic_documentary_match claims, final chunk/quotation provenance valid with three checked references, no inferences. Retrieval and extraction safeguards deployed in 2bf8b33, 458defd, 2980af3, 68e63ff, e6546a4 and f4077fa; 40 focused production tests passed.
